subject: superacid flask
title: The Strongest Acid on Earth Eats Glass, So It Lives in Plastic

scenes.text: This acid dissolves glass. So they store it in plastic.
Fluoroantimonic acid: hydrogen fluoride plus antimony pentafluoride, quadrillions of times stronger than pure sulfuric acid.
It eats through glass, so it's stored in Teflon, the non-stick pan coating.
Add water and it reacts violently. It can even force a proton onto methane.
That chemistry won George Olah the 1994 Nobel Prize, for trapping carbon ions nobody could hold before.
Glass, water, even methane. Everything reacts. Except the frying pan.

description:
Fluoroantimonic acid, a mixture of hydrogen fluoride and antimony pentafluoride, is the strongest superacid ever measured.
Its Hammett acidity is around minus 21 to minus 23, against about minus 12 for pure sulfuric acid, and popular science sources put it at 10 quadrillion to a billion billion times stronger. It dissolves glass on contact, so it is handled in PTFE, or Teflon, and it reacts violently with water. Superacids like it can force a proton onto methane, the chemistry that earned George Olah the 1994 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on carbocations.
What's the most dangerous chemical you've heard of?
first_comment: Hydrofluoric acid alone already etches glass; adding antimony pentafluoride makes it quadrillions of times stronger. Which chemical would you never want in your lab?
